title: AI and the Future of Social Work: Exploring Opportunities and Ethical Questions
location: Tate-Turner-Kuralt Building, Auditorium
description:
When thinking about the future of AI, social work may not be the first field that comes to mind. However, researchers and educators at UNC’s School of Social Work have long been engaged in AI-related projects and have unique insights to share about how the technology can be used to address important social problems.

 

This panel discussion between School of Social Work faculty will explore current and potential uses of AI in social work research and education and key ethical considerations related to its use in the field. The panelists include experts with more than a decade of experience in AI-involved research as well as relatively recent adopters of the technology.

 

This is a hybrid event. Join us at https://unc.zoom.us/j/96298278191.

 

The panel will be moderated by Kathy Colville, Associate Dean for Community Engagement and Outreach, and feature the following panelists:

 

Eric Rice
Distinguished Professor
Associate Dean of Research and Faculty Development
Gordon Berg and Martha Beach Chair in Community Social Work

Rice’s current work focuses on the application of AI technologies to assist persons living with homelessness and the organizations that serve them. For the past decade, he has worked with colleagues in computer science to merge social work science and AI, seeking novel solutions to major social problems such as homelessness, suicide, and HIV. In 2016, along with Milind Tambe, he founded the University of Southern California’s Center for AI in Society, the world’s first university-based center merging AI and social work.

 

Heidi McNeilly
Clinical Assistant Professor, Adams School of Dentistry
Adjunct Assistant Professor, School of Social Work

McNeilly’s work involves integrating social work services into dental education to enhance patient care and improve access for underserved populations, and her current research focus is the integration of AI into education. To this end, she recently led a team that developed an AI chatbot to help dental students build patient communication skills. In 2026, McNeilly was named the UNC Center for Faculty Excellence’s Faculty Fellow for Generative AI and Clinical Education. The fellowship will support her efforts to build resources related to the instructional needs and challenges presented by generative AI for faculty members campuswide.

 

Hsun-Ta Hsu
Associate Professor & John A. Tate Early Career Scholar, School of Social Work
Associate Professor, School of Data and Information Sciences

Hsu has long been interested in how artificial intelligence can help people make complex decisions with consistency, but he also recognizes the ethical and fairness challenges that AI-aided decision-making may pose for disenfranchised communities. His recent work adopts a community-engaged data science approach to promoting health and housing outcomes among individuals experiencing homelessness by engaging stakeholders to co-develop AI tools that address their most pressing needs in ways that are both efficient and equitable. Hsu also teaches courses on AI, including a new offering entitled AI for Social Good and Social Work Practice: Ethical and Applied Perspectives.

 

Stefanie Panke
Director of Digital Learning and Innovation, School of Social Work

Panke is actively engaged in researching, promoting, and advocating for the responsible and effective integration of AI—particularly generative AI—into educational practices. Her work includes research on GenAI in academic writing, teaching, and instructional design, with contributions to a Journal of Teacher Education special issue and an edited, student-authored e-book on GenAI in education. Recently, Panke and School of Social Work colleague Tina Souders were awarded a 2025–26 CFE/Lenovo Instructional Innovation Grant from the UNC Center for Faculty Excellence to support the School’s online MSW program through the use of AI to assist in the development of high-quality, immersive, and accessible multimedia learning materials, particularly case studies and simulations.

title: *IN-PERSON* SF/F Group
description:
Durham Writers Group
We will be at the People's Solidarity Hub at 1809 Chapel Hill Rd, Durham. This venue does not serve food or drink, but feel free to bring your own. There is a kitchenette for our use, but be sure to clean up afterwards. The space might be a little cozy; please consider masking or staying home if you have a respiratory ailment.

This sub-group focuses on Speculative Fiction, including Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror. If you have anything that falls under that category — be it short story, poem, novel-in-progress or screenplay — then come! We'd love to hear from you.

Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. To ensure fairness, each attendee is limited to 1 minute of Initial Feedback time. During that period, the author remains silent. Next, we have a 5 minute Free-For-All discussion about the work -- then the author may speak. (We usually get through three readers.)

Though not required, in order to receive more in-depth feed-back, readers may post their work in advance on our Google Group:
https://groups.google.com/d/forum/durham-sff-writers-group

We ask that participants keep their comments constructive and respectful, focusing on what works or doesn't work in the piece.

We also ask that readers provide a warning, both on the Google Group and during the meeting, if their story features content that some readers might find upsetting. This includes descriptions of violence or sexual content.

title: America 250 at Carolina
description:
Join us for a series of events to commemorate America's 250th anniversary at the nation's first public university. The events run from Oct. 14 to 23 and include performances, poetry readings, lectures, panel discussions and more. Most of the events are free and open to the public. 

 

Visit America 250 at Carolina on the history website. 

 

Schedule of Events

 

Wednesday, October 14

4:30-6 p.m. (Flyleaf Books) – Discussion with Antwain Hunter (History) on Frederick Douglass’s What to the Slave is the Fourth of July (1852) with Aisha Booze-Hall (Jackson Center)
Please purchase tickets for this event.

 

Monday, October 19

 

12:30-1 p.m. (Pleasants Room, Wilson Library) – Opening Keynote by Pamela Brewington Cashwell (Secretary, NCDC), North Carolina at 250

 

1-2 p.m. (Pleasants Room) – Preserving North Carolina’s History for the General Public, a panel discussion with Sec. Pamela Brewington Cashwell, Darin Waters (Dep. Sec. Office of Archives and History), and Biff Hollingsworth (Wilson Library)

 

2:15-3:30 p.m. (Pleasants Room, Wilson Library) – Teaching the Foundations of American Democracy in K-12 Schools, a panel discussion with Cori Greer Banks (Carolina K-12, CPH), Jillian La Serna (EPIC/Public Policy); and Mike Henning (Carrboro Elementary)

 

3:40-3:45 p.m. (Pleasants Room, Wilson Library) – Poetry Reading by Alexis Clifton (English and Creative Writing class of 2027), You Say the New American Dream is to Leave/Honeysuckle Dosage.

 

3:45-5 p.m. (Pleasants Room, Wilson Library) – Poetry and Liberty, a panel discussion with Tyree Daye (English and Comp Lit) Eliza Richards (English and Comp Lit), and Denise Xu (English and Comp Lit)

 

6-7:30 p.m. (Stone Center Auditorium) – Welcome by LeRhonda S. Manigault-Bryant (Director, Sonja Haynes Stone Center for Research in Black Culture and History). Poetry Reading and Conversation with Natasha Trethewey (Pulitzer-Prize Winning Former U.S. Poet Laureate), moderated by Michael A. Betts II (High Point University) and Miguel La Serna (Chair, History). SOLD OUT

 

Tuesday, October 20

6-7 p.m. (Person Recital Hall) – Welcome by Jocelyn Neal (Chair, Music). Lecture and conversation with John Wood Sweet (History), Bancroft-Prize winning author of The Sewing Girl’s Tale, moderated by Michael A. Betts II and Miguel La Serna (Chair, History)

 

7-8:30 p.m. (Person Recital Hall) – Mending Sampler: Lanah Sawyer and the Cost of Courage in Revolutionary America, a concert featuring C. Leonard Raybon (Director of Choirs, Composer at Tulane University; Founder of Sacred Nine Project), Jeanne Fisher (Music), E. NAACP Legal Defense Fund (LDF) archivists and SOHP oral historians and project leaders will explore freedom as an ongoing and active pursuit

title: Engagement in Research Nuts & Bolts
description:
Engagement in Research Nuts & Bolts: Specific Approaches for Engaging Patient & Community Partners in Research

 

There is no "one-size-fits-all" approach to engaging patient, community, or other partners in your research. Rather, there are a variety of engagement methods to suit your study's needs, your research team's capacity, and your partners' interests.

 

This online training will describe three common approaches for working with patient, community, and other partners in your research: 1) consultative community feedback sessions; 2) advisory boards; and 3) sustained collaboration with partners as members of the research team.

 

The session will cover considerations for choosing these specific engagement methods, as well as concrete processes and steps for implementing each approach. Participation in our Engagement in Research 101 training is not required to attend this session; however, some knowledge of engagement, whether from prior training(s) or personal experience, may foster deeper understanding of the material in this session.

 

Register

 

Presenters:
Alicia Bilheimer, MPH - Director of Engaged Science, NC TraCS
Veronica Carlisle, MPH, CHES - Senior Community Health Educator, UNC Lineberger Comprehensive Cancer Center (LCCC)
Nisha Datta, MS - Senior Project Manager, NC TraCS
Simone Frank, MPH - Senior Project Manager, NC TraCS
Jennifer Potter, MPH, CHES - Senior Program Coordinator for Clinical Outreach, LCCC

 

Engaging Patient, Community, and Other Partners in Your Research is a multi-part online training series. You may register for the entire series OR any single training session. This training series was developed collaboratively with patient, community, and researcher partners and is co-sponsored by the UNC Lineberger Comprehensive Cancer Center and NC TraCS Institute.

description:
Brain Chemistry and ADHD: What We Know and Where We Are Headed

Brain structure and brain chemistry are crucial components to understanding ADHD and its treatment.  Greg Mattingly, M.D., is the President of the American Professional Society of ADHD and Related Disorders (APSARD), has served as consultant to both the NFL and MLB, and is Co-Chair of the U.S. Psych Congress. He has extensively researched ADHD and taught psychopharmacology for more than 20 years. In this seminar he will bring his wealth of knowledge and expertise to present what is known about brain function and ADHD, including how various brain chemicals such as dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin are involved. He will offer current research findings, will address how medications to treat ADHD are related to brain neuroanatomy and neurotransmitters, and will discuss new and upcoming medication options. The presentation will also include information on brain neuroplasticity, environmental influences, accompanying diagnoses, and the new adult guidelines for diagnosing ADHD.

title: Sacred Nine Project: Mending Sampler
location: Person Hall, Recital Hall
description:
FEATURING

Diya Kayaleh, soprano
Beth Allen-Gardner, mezzo-soprano
Henry Reacher, tenor
Liam O’Laughlin, baritone
C. Leonard Raybon, baritone
Danny Spiegel, piano

 

PROGRAM

Sacred Nine Project: Mending Sampler

Sacred Nine Project is excited to celebrate John Wood Sweet’s, The Sewing Girl’s Tale, with a curated vocal concert at The University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, where he is Professor of History.

Content warning: descriptions of rape and suicide

“Cost of courage,” is Sweet’s turn of phrase. He writes:

As a young woman, Lanah Sawyer had a rare kind of courage.  Only seventeen, a stepchild in a working family, she was easy to dismiss as a mere “sewing girl.”  Yet, when an affluent gentleman showed an interest in her, she dared to image that he might really be interested in her.  Violently, he dashed that dream—leaving her disoriented, distressed, and unmoored.  Then, she gathered her courage and did what no one else in the nation’s biggest city had done in half a century: she charged a gentleman with rape.  Then, as now, most survivors of sexual assaults by acquaintances don’t make any official complaint—and for good reason. But Lanah Sawyer refused to be shamed. She refused to be silenced. What followed was a harrowing ordeal—and a remarkable vindication.  THE SEWING GIRL’S TALE is the story of this remarkable young woman’s search for justice, her determination to move beyond what had been done to her, to rebuild her life—to live with the courage of her conviction that she, too, was someone who mattered.

Raybon is drawing on historical sources, early American music, and newly written poetry for the presentation. One historical source is Report of the Trial of Henry Bedlow for Committing a Rape on Lanah Sawyer, New York, 1793, by William Wyche; this is a first-hand account of the trial. Charlotte Temple: A Tale of Truth (1791) by Susanna Rowson, containing a narrative not unlike the present account, is a further historical writing. Still another early text, The American Spelling Book (originally published in 1783) by Noah Webster, offers poetry and prose that might shed light on the kind of shame-and-gender-based education that a girl like Lanah would have received. A 1794 tune book, The Harmony of Maine (1794), compiled by Supply Belcher, offers inspiration from the Song of Songs, in which “the voice of my beloved” is seductive, and in our case, dangerous. Finally, Lanah’s story will incite brand new verse to honor her and her legacy.

 

PARKING

Please plan to arrive early as parking on campus can be tricky. Learn more about parking and directions to UNC-Chapel Hill’s campus.

This event is co-sponsored by the Department of Music and the Department of History.

Please join our virtual welcome session with this link

Are you a young person between 13 and 25 years old who is interested in taking action around preventing gun violence? Join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session to learn more about the different ways you can engage. 

Team ENOUGH is a youth-led program whose mission is to educate young voices about gun violence and mobilize them to take meaningful action against it. Supported by Brady United, we harness the expertise and experience of today’s youth to advance our intersectional work across the country. 

Led by an Executive Council, comprised of students just like us, we believe that diversity is a strength, and that only when everyone has a seat at the table can we build an effective movement to prevent all gun violence in all communities.

For us, preventing gun violence not only requires regulating access to firearms but also addressing how systemic racism and environmental factors cause this form of bloodshed to run especially rampant in communities of color. You cannot talk about gun violence without talking about police brutality, white supremacy, the broken criminal justice system, poverty, homophobia, access to affordable housing, or the often barriers separating disadvantaged populations from physical and mental healthcare. 

So if you share this belief, join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session and become part of the movement to end gun violence in our lifetime.

title: Alexi Kenney, violin Shifting Ground Projection art by Xuan
location: Hill Hall, Moeser Auditorium
description:
How can the way we listen change when music is presented as part of a continuing story, rather than one moment in time? Does it make us feel more open, flexible, or curious?

 

Being in the audience for Shifting Ground might feel a bit like standing on the bank of a flowing river: being able to look toward what is coming or to turn and see what has passed, all from one vantage point.

 

Violinist Alexi Kenney invites audiences into this time-traveling musical journey which includes works by J.S. Bach interwoven with those of contemporary creators, including Rafiq Bhatia, Kaija Saariaho, Paul Wiancko, Salina Fisher and Angélica Negrón—all accompanied by projection art by Xuan. Along the way, audiences encounter deeply affecting moments including a work that pairs solo violin with the recorded sounds of a melting glacier. 

 

As music and imagery unfold together, familiar sounds take on new meaning and unexpected connections emerge. The result is an experience of music as a living conversation across generations that rewards deep listening.

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/shiftingground/

It's time to play the third annual Cyber Bowl, a month-long competition to determine which North Carolina university is the most cyber savvy. 

 

All October long, students, faculty and staff can log into the Cyber Bowl website and take a short cybersecurity quiz. Each completed quiz earns a point for Carolina.

 

UNC-Chapel Hill faces off against nine other North Carolina universities with a lot to prove and two wins to defend. In the inaugural Cyber Bowl, Carolina won the championship by garnering the largest participation by percentage. Last year, Carolina fielded the most players — almost 2,000 — of any school.

title: UNC Research Week
location: Campus Wide
description:
UNC Research Week (URW) will return October 19-23, 2026, with the theme “What’s Next?”
 

This year, we will showcase emerging ideas, discoveries, and innovations at Carolina that are shaping our future. Join us in highlighting the Carolina research community’s commitment to advancing knowledge that has the potential to transform industries, strengthen communities, and create a better world for us all. From breakthroughs in materials science to novel AI applications to creative and cultural exploration, we’re diving into endeavors that are at the frontier of what’s known.

title: Oct 22 - Advances in AI at Virginia Tech
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from AI researchers at Virginia Tech!

**Date, Time and Location**

Oct 22, 2026
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
**[Online. Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/advances-in-ai-at-virginia-tech-october-22-2026)**

**Multi-Agent Communication: A framework, diagnostic and mechanistic perspective**

Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly used for collaborative reasoning, debate, and consensus, yet their communication dynamics remain poorly understood. This talk presents a framework for studying multi-agent communication through diagnostic and mechanistic perspectives.

I will discuss CONSENSAGENT, which improves consensus by mitigating sycophancy, alongside our diagnostic work on communication patterns and failure modes in real-world multi-agent debates. I will then present ongoing work that moves toward a mechanistic understanding of how these interaction patterns arise internally, with the broader goal of making multi-agent systems more interpretable, reliable, and controllable.

*About the Speaker*

[Priya Pitre](https://www.linkedin.com/in/priya-p-a31360117/) I am an Ph.D student in the Computer Science Department at Virginia Tech (VT), co-advised by Dr. Xuan Wang and Dr. Naren Ramakrishnan.

**Exposing and Improving Fine-Grained Visual Grounding Abilities of Lightweight Multimodal LLMs**

Lightweight multimodal LLMs can localize whole objects effectively, yet often struggle when a query targets a small object part or fine-grained visual detail. This talk presents a reasoning-guided framework that teaches compact models to ground parts through an explicit coarse-to-fine process: first locating the parent object, then identifying the requested part.

A part-aware reinforcement-learning objective provides stage-wise rewards for object accuracy, part containment, and the consistency of the model’s self-critique. Using these techniques, a compact 4B-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot part grounding while preserving its object-level performance.

These advances can be used to enable lightweight MLLMs to support detail-oriented tasks in biology and robotics.

*About the Speaker*

[Kazi Mehrab ](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ksmehrab/)I a CS PhD candidate at Virginia Tech, where I currently focus on multimodal LLMs and computer vision tasks, including visual perception, reasoning and grounding.

**Understanding Visual Generative Models for Precise Control**

Despite remarkable progress in image and video generation, translating user intent into precise and consistent visual outputs remains a challenge. This talk explores how understanding the representations within generative models can enable finer control over what they create.

It connects semantic image editing with compositional generation, examining how visual concepts can be isolated, manipulated, and combined while preserving their identity and surrounding content. Building on these insights, structured visual inputs provide a way to express complex intent through subject references, poses, and spatial layouts.

The discussion then extends from images to video, where representations must evolve to preserve scene continuity while accommodating motion and change. Together, these directions establish a unified perspective on how visual representations can support controllable editing, composition, and coherent generation across space and time.

*About the Speaker*

[Yusuf Dalva](https://www.linkedin.com/in/yusuf-dalva/) is a Ph.D. candidate at Virginia Tech, advised by Pinar Yanardag and affiliated with the Sanghani Center for Artificial Intelligence and Data Analytics.

location: Carolina Union, 2502
description:
The POP Lab is a drop-in workspace where UNC faculty and staff can make progress with support from digital accessibility consultants. Bring your documents, course materials, websites, reports, or questions, and work at your own pace. Come by for a few minutes or stay for the full session to ask questions, explore tools, solve problems and make meaningful progress toward expanding access.

 

Progress Over Perfection

Progress means recognizing common barriers in the platforms you use and taking small steps to reduce them. It’s choosing web formats over PDFs, applying table headers, checking color contrast and collaborating on accessible templates so everyone can start from a strong foundation. Digital accessibility depends on steady, intentional progress, not perfection, to expand access for all.

title: America 250 at Carolina
description:
Join us for a series of events to commemorate America's 250th anniversary at the nation's first public university. The events run from Oct. 14 to 23 and include performances, poetry readings, lectures, panel discussions and more. Most of the events are free and open to the public. 

 

Visit America 250 at Carolina on the history website. 

 

Schedule of Events

 

Wednesday, October 14

4:30-6 p.m. (Flyleaf Books) – Discussion with Antwain Hunter (History) on Frederick Douglass’s What to the Slave is the Fourth of July (1852) with Aisha Booze-Hall (Jackson Center)
Please purchase tickets for this event.

 

Monday, October 19

 

12:30-1 p.m. (Pleasants Room, Wilson Library) – Opening Keynote by Pamela Brewington Cashwell (Secretary, NCDC), North Carolina at 250

 

1-2 p.m. (Pleasants Room) – Preserving North Carolina’s History for the General Public, a panel discussion with Sec. Pamela Brewington Cashwell, Darin Waters (Dep. Sec. Office of Archives and History), and Biff Hollingsworth (Wilson Library)

 

2:15-3:30 p.m. (Pleasants Room, Wilson Library) – Teaching the Foundations of American Democracy in K-12 Schools, a panel discussion with Cori Greer Banks (Carolina K-12, CPH), Jillian La Serna (EPIC/Public Policy); and Mike Henning (Carrboro Elementary)

 

3:40-3:45 p.m. (Pleasants Room, Wilson Library) – Poetry Reading by Alexis Clifton (English and Creative Writing class of 2027), You Say the New American Dream is to Leave/Honeysuckle Dosage.

 

3:45-5 p.m. (Pleasants Room, Wilson Library) – Poetry and Liberty, a panel discussion with Tyree Daye (English and Comp Lit) Eliza Richards (English and Comp Lit), and Denise Xu (English and Comp Lit)

 

6-7:30 p.m. (Stone Center Auditorium) – Welcome by LeRhonda S. Manigault-Bryant (Director, Sonja Haynes Stone Center for Research in Black Culture and History). Poetry Reading and Conversation with Natasha Trethewey (Pulitzer-Prize Winning Former U.S. Poet Laureate), moderated by Michael A. Betts II (High Point University) and Miguel La Serna (Chair, History). SOLD OUT

 

Tuesday, October 20

10 a.m. - Noon (Pleasants Room, Wilson Library) – Great American Stories: Food, Music, and Folklore of the American South with Amanda J. Cobb (American Studies), Kelly Alexander (American Studies), and Gabrielle Berlinger (American Studies)

 

2:30-4 p.m. (Pleasants Room, Wilson Library) – Lecture and conversation with David Crabtree (CEO and General Manager, PBS North Carolina), moderated by Michael A. Betts II

 

5-5:30 p.m. (Playmakers Lobby) – Colonial Fiddling by Eli Howells

 

5:30-7 p.m. (Playmakers) – Lecture by Mandy Cooper (History) Hamilton in Historical Context. Conversation with Daveed Diggs, a Tony, Grammy, and Lucille Lortel Award-winning actor, writer, producer, and musician best known for originating the dual roles of Thomas Jefferson and Marquis de Lafayette in the original cast of the Broadway hit Hamilton, earning a Tony Award for his performance. Moderated by Michael A. Betts II (High Point University), Miguel La Serna (Chair, History), and Katherine Hunter Williams (Chair, Dramatic Arts). Limited tickets will be available by sponsoring departments.

 

Wednesday, October 21

2:30-3:30 p.m. (Pleasants Room, Wilson Library) – Lecture by Katherine Turk (History), “All Men Would be Tyrants if They Could”: Women and Power in Revolutionary America

 

3:45-4:30 p.m. (Pleasants Room, Wilson Library) – Performance by Singer-Songwriter Dawn Landes, The Liberated Woman’s Songbook

 

6-7 p.m. (Person Recital Hall) – Welcome by Jocelyn Neal (Chair, Music). Lecture and conversation with John Wood Sweet (History), Bancroft-Prize winning author of The Sewing Girl’s Tale, moderated by Michael A. Betts II and Miguel La Serna (Chair, History)

 

7-8:30 p.m. (Person Recital Hall) – Mending Sampler: Lanah Sawyer and the Cost of Courage in Revolutionary America, a concert featuring C. Leonard Raybon (Director of Choirs, Composer at Tulane University; Founder of Sacred Nine Project), Jeanne Fisher (Music), E. Katherine Hargrove (Colonial Williamsburg interpreter), and undergraduate performers (Music)

 

Thursday, October 22

2:30-3:30 p.m. (University Room, Hyde Hall) – Lecture by Wayne E. Lee (History), The Cutting-Off Way: Indigenous Warfare in the American Revolution

 

3:45-4:45 p.m. (University Room, Hyde Hall) – Lecture by Amanda J. Cobb (American Studies), Indigenous Perspectives on America 250 Memory and Commemoration

 

6:30 – 8:30 p.m. (Fearrington Reading Room, Wilson Library) Lecture by Kathleen DuVal (History), author of Native Nations, North Carolina and the War for Independence

 

Friday, October 23

11:30 a.m. – 12:30 p.m. (Love House) – Southern Cultures: Black Freedom Narratives in Place, Publication, and Performance, a conversation between Michelle Lanier (Director, North Carolina Historic Sites), Danielle Purifoy (Geography)and artist and activist Toshi Reagon (NYFA)

1–2 p.m. (Love House) – Lecture by Danita Mason-Hogans (Southern Oral History Program), The Role of Oral History and Community Memory in Interpreting Early American History and its Long Afterlives

 

2:15-3:30 p.m. (Love House) – SOHP and Civil Rights: Partnering with LDF
NAACP Legal Defense Fund (LDF) archivists and SOHP oral historians and project leaders will explore freedom as an ongoing and active pursuit

 

4-5:30 p.m. (Moeser Performance Hall) Theatrical Performance and Conversation with Mike Wiley (Director and Artist in Residence for the Kenan Institute for Ethics),One Noble Journey: A Box Marked Freedom

 

7:30-8:30 p.m. (Moeser Performance Hall) Concert by LaToya Lain (Music), Narrative of a Slave Woman, moderated by Michael A. Betts II

description:
It's time to play the third annual Cyber Bowl, a month-long competition to determine which North Carolina university is the most cyber savvy. 

 

All October long, students, faculty and staff can log into the Cyber Bowl website and take a short cybersecurity quiz. Each completed quiz earns a point for Carolina.

 

UNC-Chapel Hill faces off against nine other North Carolina universities with a lot to prove and two wins to defend. title: Sustainable Labs Interest Session
description:
Campus labs and research are incredibly important to the University, but they're also very water and energy intensive. In fact, campus labs are the largest consumers of water and energy on campus. Started in 2009 as the Green Labs program, Sustainable Carolina has revamped the program and given it a new name: Sustainable Labs.

 

The program focuses on key areas (waste, energy and water, freezers, chemicals), and is designed not to shame labs or lab personnel for waste or energy intensive equipment, but rather to identify small steps labs can take to be more sustainable and to recognize all the steps that labs have already taken.

 

This interest session for Sustainable Labs will be led by Langley Smith, Sustainable Carolina’s program specialist. We invite lab managers, students who work in labs, and faculty to join us and learn how their labs can participate in the program.

Participants will discover low-maintenance design strategies, plant combinations that thrive together and practical tips for maximizing harvests while maintaining curb appeal. Perfect for beginners and seasoned gardeners alike. 
Fee: $22; free for Duke Gardens members with discount code.

title: Carolina History Tour
description:
Learn more about the history of the nation’s first public university by attending a Carolina History Tour. The Carolina History Tours cover more than 200 years of the history of UNC-Chapel Hill, including the establishment of the university in the 18th century, the history of campus landmarks including the Old Well, Davie Poplar, and Unsung Founders Memorial, the push to open enrollment to all North Carolinians, and the growth of the school in the 20th and 21st centuries. Tours will begin at the Old Well and finish at Wilson Library. Most tours last a little over an hour. 

Led by staff from the Wilson Special Collections Library, these tours are part of the University Library’s commitment to collecting, preserving, and sharing the history of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. 

Registration is required. You can register for your spot here.

title: Educator Trek: Got Elk?
location: In the Field
description:
Join us as we search for the majestic elk, reintroduced to the Great Smoky Mountains National Park after an absence of more than 200 years. Observe and learn about elk biology, while also exploring other facets of the Park’s ecosystem. Sample some activities used to document the biodiversity of the Park. Participate in citizen science data collection on snails and lichens. Discover how you can bring the excitement of field research into your classroom. 
Credit: 20 contact hours toward CEUs or Criteria II/III for North Carolina’s Environmental Education Certification Program 
Lodging: The workshop fee covers a two-night stay in a lodge in Lake Junaluska, NC. Most rooms will be double occupancy. 
Transportation: Participants can ride with the group from Raleigh departing at 2pm or meet us at the lodging in Lake Junaluska in the evening. Transportation will be in Museum vans. 
Registration: This workshop is FULL, please join our waiting list! 
The full workshop fee is due when you register and payment is via credit card. Registration for most Educator Treks is on a first-come, first-served basis. Treks fill quickly, so register early! title: Mike Wiley: One Noble Journey
location: Hill Hall, Moeser Auditorium
description:
FEATURING

Mike Wiley

Mike Wiley holds a Masters of Fine Arts from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and was the 2010 and 2014 Lehman Brady Visiting Joint Chair Professor in Documentary Studies and American Studies at Duke University and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Wiley received the University of North Carolina’s Distinguished Alumni Award in 2017.

 

PROGRAM

One Noble Journey

Henry “Box” Brown was an African American born into slavery in 1816 in Louisa County, Virginia. Although he was not subjected to physical violence, Henry’s story (the basis for One Noble Journey) demonstrates the cruelty of slavery was every bit as devastating to the heart as it could be on the body.After his family was torn apart and parceled out to various beneficiaries of the estate, Henry devised an ingenious escape plan – sealing himself in a wooden box for shipment to friends and freedom in Philadelphia.

One Noble Journey also recounts the daring and miraculous quest for freedom of Elizabeth Craft and her husband William, who were born into slavery in Georgia.* Ellen Craft, who was very light skinned, disguised herself as a sickly, white gentleman traveling to Philadelphia for medical treatment. Ellen and William, who acted as her slave throughout the journey, bravely traveled on public trains and steamers as they made their way up the eastern seaboard to Philadelphia. Eventually they were forced to sail for England after the Fugitive Slave Law enabled slave hunters to pursue them even in free states.

 

PARKING

title: Narrative of a Slave Woman: Songs of Hope, Justice, and Freedom
location: Hill Hall, Moeser Auditorium
description:
FEATURING

LaToya Lain, soprano

 

PROGRAM

A powerful presentation by soprano LaToya Lain that examines the issue of slavery by combining musical performance with spoken narrative accounts. About the project, Lain says, “In 2003, HBO presented a documentary entitled ‘Unchained Memories’ about the stories of former slaves interviewed during the 1930s’ Federal Writers’ Project. As I read the print version of these slave narratives and later watched the documentary, I began to see how the stories of these men and women are told through the Negro Spirituals. I saw the direct relationship of some of my favorite spirituals and the life stories of remarkable slave women, whose names, if not for these narratives, we would have never known. I was inspired to take these narratives and combine them with concert arranged Negro Spirituals to tell the story of one former slave woman through song.”

title: Native Tree Planting (Cornelius)
description:
Join NCWF Lake Norman Wildlife Chapter to plant native trees in Cornelius as part of North Carolina Wildlife Federation’s Clean and Green program. Back in April, NCWF Lake Norman Wildlife Chapter and the Town of Cornelius hosted its annual Clean & Green trash cleanup event. Town staff and volunteers from the Society of Women Engineers, Safe Harbor – Kings Point Marina, and Lake Norman Wildlife took to the land and the lake to remove hundreds of pounds of trash and debris. 
North Carolina Wildlife Federation is committed to planting one native tree for every 25 pounds of trash collected statewide. Removing litter protects wildlife from possible entanglement, strangulation, and ingestion while improving water quality and removing toxins from the environment. 
This year we will plant native trees at Bailey Road Park. Trees are the foundation of our terrestrial food webs, and they provide critical nesting habitat for owls, hawks, songbirds, and other wildlife. Please join us at Bailey Road Park for a morning of community and conservation. Stick around for pizza, refreshments, and a group photo at the end. 
Volunteers will work to prepare the existing holes before planting and mulching up to 80 native trees. 
Children under 18 must be accompanied by a parent or guardian. 
Please reach out to Billy Wilson, President – Lake Norman Wildlife, with questions at billy.wilson@LNWC.org, or 704-675-2011

title: Sunday Community Game Day at The Can Opener
description:
Durham Geeks
What is up, my fellow humans?! Need somewhere to go or something to do this Sunday afternoon? How do some good games, good people, and good food sound??? I thought so. You want to be here!

Come join us at our new (hopefully permanent) spot, The Can Opener, for some Sunday afternoon board gaming shenanigans! As always, we always bring an egregious number of games, so feel free to come in and let us teach you something new! Even if you’re new to board games or just want to try something new, we will get you a seat and make sure you don’t have to stumble through a rulebook. Of course, you are more than welcome to bring a game of your own to play if you’re a seasoned gamer (or just really love that ONE game!) we will get it to the table!

The Can Opener has a ton of great food options from one of their food trucks. There is also a great selection of snacks inside along with great coffee and whatever beverage(s) you may want! The spot is cozy, well lit, dog friendly, and super inclusive, not to mention that we have a great group of friends that will make you feel right at home! Can't ask for much more than that.

So come on out and let's show The Can Opener some of that good Durham Game Community LOVE!

title: ecoEXPLORE Shifting Species: Climate & Behavior and Arachnid Costume Party (Columbia)
description:
Can you think of ways that wildlife might respond to changes in climate? During our ecoEXPLORE “Shifting Species” program, NCWF, Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge, and Tyrrell County Library will dive into how species shift their behavior in response to changes in weather vs. climate as we work to complete our Climate Badge Challenge 3! Join us as we learn more about local and regional examples of wildlife and plants that have adapted due to changes in their environment. 
To celebrate the end of the Arachnology Field Season, ecoEXPLORErs are invited to wear their arachnid costumes from the Arachnology Badge Challenge 3! Don’t feel like dressing up? That’s okay, we’d love to see a sketch of your costume design instead! 
ecoEXPLORE is a community science program, created by the North Carolina Arboretum, where children of all ages are able to learn how to identify wildlife around them, help real scientists track wildlife activity, and earn fun badges and prizes all at the same time! To learn more about ecoEXPLORE, please visit https://www.ecoexplore.net/.

title: Building Partnerships for Innovation: A Fireside Chat with Vice Chancellor Tommy Sowers
location: 79 Degrees West
description:
Join Innovate Carolina for a fireside conversation with Tommy Sowers, Vice Chancellor for Innovation, Entrepreneurship and Economic Development at UNC Chapel Hill, about UNC's role in building stronger partnerships across North Carolina and supporting innovation and economic development in the region. Hosted at 79°West in Pittsboro, the conversation will focus on the growing opportunities to connect UNC with communities, entrepreneurs and North Carolina based companies throughout Central North Carolina. 

 

Chatham County and Pittsboro are an important part of this regional ecosystem, creating opportunities for UNC to build stronger relationships with the communities and companies surrounding the university. The conversation will also highlight UNC's Industry Partnerships Initiative and its focus on developing meaningful relationships with North Carolina companies. Together, these partnerships can connect companies with UNC's talent, research, innovation and entrepreneurial resources while creating opportunities for greater economic impact across the state. 

 

Come hear Vice Chancellor Sowers share his perspective on Carolina's role in the region, the opportunities ahead for Central North Carolina, and how stronger partnerships can benefit both the university and the communities around it.

title: Price Cone Liptzin Lecture with Guy Mossman
location: Carroll Hall, Knight Learning Lab (Carroll Hall 111)
description:
Hosted by the UNC Hussman School of Journalism and Media, the fall 2026 Price Cone Liptzin Lecture will feature alumnus Guy Mossman ’04 (M.A.), an American cinematographer whose work bridges intimate character study with bold, cinematic visuals.

 

Mossman made his first short film while serving in the Peace Corps in Paraguay in 2000 and went on to earn a Park Fellowship at UNC-Chapel Hill, completing a master’s degree focused on journalism and documentary filmmaking. 

 

He is known for his dramatic, natural-light photography on award-winning documentaries including the Oscar-shortlisted Sundance Audience Award winner “Buck,” the Sundance Special Jury Prize-winning “Feels Good Man” and “Bending the Arc.”

 

In 2022, he made his directorial debut co-directing and lensing “The Human Trial,” an ambitious, years-long chronicle of a radical Type 1 diabetes clinical trial. Most recently, he co-directed, produced and photographed SPEAK., a feature documentary that premiered at the 2025 Sundance Film Festival, following teenage competitive orators at the National Speech & Debate Association’s championship as they discover the power of their voices through oratory and storytelling.

 

Registration

RSVP on Eventbrite

UNC students can register for CLE credit on Heel Life

 

About Mary Jane Price and Annie Cone Liptzin

The visual communication alumni-in-residence series was created in honor of Mary Jane Price and Annie Cone Liptzin, alumnae who volunteered for nearly a decade to assist with the darkroom, equipment checkout and other needs of the UNC Hussman visual journalism program beginning in the 1980s.

title: Narrative Analysis for the Qualitative Researcher (online)
description:
This course features Dynamic Narrative Inquiry – theory and principles for narrative research design and analysis drawing on the richness of expressive language. With this approach to qualitative inquiry, researchers can build on communication in daily life where diverse practices for sharing experience, making sense of experience, and imagining social change occur in personal narratives, sociocultural communications, and institutional policies.

This course involves a sequence of presentations and practical workshops with narrative analysis strategies applicable to small or large studies that sample verbal and/or visual discourse. We begin with an introduction to dynamic narrative inquiry, followed by modules with three analysis strategies that yield findings to a wide range of relevant social science research questions. With examples from prior published studies, I present rationales and methodology, including character mapping (to identify meaning in narrative actors, actions, and relationships); plot analysis (to identify how narrative structures express logics and intentions); and values analysis (to identify speaker/author/ purposes). The final hour of the day is devoted to discussing course participants’ insights from the workshops and implications for future research, practice, and policy.

Registration and fee (refundable for students) are required for Zoom link.

title: Managing The Emotions Surrounding Layoff Conversations
description:
Delivering layoff messages generates a range of emotions for both the manager delivering the message and the employee receiving it. As a manager, you may feel guilt over having to be the bearer of such bad news. You may feel fear from many sources: fear about your own job security, fear about the impact the announcement will have on others, and fear about how the employee might react during the conversation. Some managers also feel anger, which could be directed toward senior leadership or others responsible for putting managers and the company in this difficult position. All of these emotions are normal and expected. This training helps you better understand these emotions so that you can stay in control of the situation and do your best, instead of allowing the emotions to take over and negatively impact the conversation and your own well-being.

title: Agent Orchestration in the Enterprise: Coordination, Control, and Scale
description:
Data Science Raleigh
As enterprises move from isolated AI assistants to interconnected agentic systems, orchestration is becoming a critical layer of the AI stack. Coordinating multiple agents across tools, data sources, models, and workflows introduces new opportunities for automation—but also new challenges around reliability, governance, observability, and control.

This session explores what it takes to design and operationalize agent orchestration in enterprise environments. From assigning roles and managing handoffs to monitoring performance and enforcing guardrails, we’ll examine how organizations can build coordinated agent systems that scale without sacrificing trust, security, or human oversight.

**You’ll Learn:**

* From Agents to Systems: How orchestration enables multiple agents, models, tools, and workflows to work together toward shared business objectives.
* Coordination and Handoffs: Approaches for assigning tasks, managing dependencies, resolving conflicts, and maintaining context across agents.
* Control and Observability: How to monitor agent behavior, evaluate performance, and intervene when workflows break down or produce unexpected outcomes.
* Scaling Responsibly: Strategies for governing, securing, and scaling agentic systems while maintaining accountability and appropriate human oversight.

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Difficult Conversations During Times of Unrest
description:
Millions of people have read about and watched footage from recent tragic events. It’s normal for these events to generate strong feelings that can carry over to conversations at home and in the workplace. Conversations about polarizing issues can be tense or even destructive, but avoiding such conversations is not always a good solution. In this webinar, we discuss ways to have healthy discussions about polarizing topics without damaging your important relationships. We’ll also discuss productive ways to talk about the events with children.

title: Guided Tour and Meditation with Maya Freelon
location: Gregg Museum of Art & Design
description:
Join artist Maya Freelon for an immersive gallery tour of Grounded, exploring the evolution of her work, creative practice, and the Freelon lineage and legacy. Through conversation, "slow looking", gentle movement, awareness, and discovery, participants will engage with the textures, colors, materials, and memories embedded in Freelon’s work.

The tour will include artwork by Maya Freelon, alongside photographs by her late father, Phil Freelon — NC State Design School alum and architect of the renovated Gregg Museum of Art & Design — and her great-grandfather, Allan Freelon, Sr., a pioneer African American Impressionist painter active during the Harlem Renaissance.

The exhibition space welcomes the practice of grounding, as Maya guides visitors through mindful moments that evoke the senses and invite reflection on ancestry, healing, joy, resilience, and connection. title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: IAH Fellows Forum: Antonia Randolph
location: Hyde Hall, University Room
description:
On Oct. 30, American studies Assistant Professor Antonia Randolph (FFP ’22) will give a Fellows Forum presentation titled “It’s All Love? Beyoncé and Jay-Z and the Re-enchantment of Black Romance in the Age of the Manosphere.”

 

This talk will examine Jay-Z and Beyoncé’s post-2010 output, with an emphasis on Everything Is Love (The Carters, 2018) and Renaissance (Beyoncé, 2022), to show how their defense of romantic love converts their need to salvage their brand as hip-hop and R&B’s happily married power couple into a story about saving the Black nation through heteronormative marriage.

 

To satisfy R&B audiences, they infuse their marriage with Black nationalist significance, with its survival serving as a proxy for the survival of the Black nation. They link social mobility and wealth with heteronormative marriage, simultaneously turning marriage into an aspirational luxury item while encouraging people to look to marriage, rather than the state, to escape poverty.

 

At the same time, they satisfy hip-hop’s norms by constructing Beyoncé as uniquely deserving of empathy as the ultimate “ride or die” chick, denying that other Black women deserve the care and consideration she receives. These individualized, anti-redistributive responses to shifting gender norms and the erosion of the social safety net in the post-Civil Rights Era provide a cultural commonsense that supports the Black manosphere.

 

Antonia Randolph is the Jonathan M. Hess Career Development Term Assistant Professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Her interests include diversity discourse in education, Black feminist thought, non-normative Black masculinity and sexuality, and hip-hop culture. Her book, The Wrong Kind of Different: Challenging the Meaning of Diversity in American Classrooms (Teachers College Press, 2012), examined the hierarchies elementary school teachers constructed among students of color. Her current book project, That’s My Heart: Queering Intimacy in Hip-Hop Culture, forthcoming from the University of California Press, examines portrayals of Black men’s intimate relationships in hip-hop culture.

description:
This North Carolina State Natural Area is a gem, with a diversity of natural plant and animal communities not found anywhere else in the Triangle region. Join Paul Manos, Duke biology professor and Duke Herbarium curator, and Alec Motten, professor emeritus, Duke University Department of Biology, on a two- to three-mile mountain hike of moderate difficulty. Both Alec and Paul bring a deep expertise in plants and ecology; they will “read” the landscape and give you a unique view of Occoneechee Mountain. Please wear comfortable clothes and good walking shoes. Bring a lunch and beverage to enjoy and continue the conversation after the hike. 
Fee: $38; 20% discount for Duke Gardens members with discount code. 
Parking: Free parking available. 
Location: Occoneechee Mountain. Driving directions will be sent with the reminder for participants to meet at the site. 
Accessibility: This will be a small group program that takes place outdoors traveling on unpaved paths with some uneven surfaces and steep inclines. This walk includes a ~400’ elevation gain from the Eno River to the viewpoint.

title: Carolina North Forest Gravel + Gab
description:
Triangle Off Road Cyclists (TORC)
* **Title:** Carolina North Forest Gravel + Gab
* **Intended audience:** The gravel curious to the gravel enthusiast. This is a beginnermediate-level (\*see distance & pace below), no-drop (no one is left behind) ride from Back Alley Bikes over to the gravel roads of Carolina North Forest. Riders with gravel experience are welcome, but **we will prioritize good vibes and comfortable group riding** over speed and intensity.
* **Distance:** 15 miles ([route](https://ridewithgps.com/routes/54012358))
* **Pace:** 10-12 mph and conversational
* **Duration:** About 2.5 hours
* **Meet** @8:45am @ [Back Alley Bikes](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Vg8FUof42TmzNb6F6), **Wheels rolling** @ 9am
* Helmets are required
* ***Hot days are dangerous! Please come hydrated, bring plenty of water, and tell a leader if you feel dizzy, lightheaded, clammy, fatigued, cramps, or nausea.***
* **Please fill out the [2026 TORC ride waiver](https://www.torc-nc.org/waiver/).** You only need fill it out 1 time per year.
* Other attire: Attire is good, yes, and whatever floats your boat. Some of us ride in boots, some clip in. Dress for the weather/conditions.
* Water bottle/pack, mini-tool, spare tube/tubeless supplies, and pump/CO2 highly recommended.
* No headphones or other distractions
* Optional coffee and pastries after the ride at [Even Dough Bakery](https://www.evendough.net/_files/ugd/25157a_c98496ddedb04409a2c90324cfab6a22.pdf) (subject to change day-of)
* Message me with any questions you may have.

**HOW TO HELP TORC HELP YOU:**
If you aren't a member of TORC please consider joining. Trails are not cheap to build or easy to maintain. So much goes on behind the scenes at all the trails. If you love trails please [consider joining TORC](https://www.torc-nc.org/join-torc/) to help support the work TORC does. Not ready to join? You can [donate to TORC](https://www.torc-nc.org/join-torc/) to support our mission at the bottom of that page.

title: Jenny Elder Fitch Memorial Lecture: Digging Deeper into Ecological Horticulture
location: North Carolina Botanical Garden, 100 Old Mason Farm Road, Chapel Hill, NC, 27517, United States
description:
Speaker: Uli Lorimer, Director of Horticulture, Native Plant Trust 
Free; preregistration required 
Join us for this year’s Jenny Elder Fitch Memorial Lecture as Uli Lorimer with the Native Plant Trust explores the questions and challenges shaping ecological horticulture today. 
Successful gardens are being asked to be both beautiful and to provide ecological function. Welcoming more native plants into designed spaces has been shown to provide great benefit for humans and wildlife alike. Environmentally conscious garden decisions are based on assumptions that native plants better support ecosystems, that genetic diversity is essential, and that native cultivars may not be as functional as species. 
This talk will explore the assumptions and the challenges to those assumptions. What role does the nursery industry play in providing the right kinds of information for gardeners to make informed decisions? Do maintenance practices influence biodiversity, and how do science and research factor into these assumptions?

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: The Bettie Allison Rand Lectures in Art History: Alexander Marr, University of Cambridge
location: Hyde Hall, University Room
description:
Pictorial Intelligence in Renaissance Art: Holbein’s Wit

 

The Renaissance witnessed intense debate about the nature and location of human intelligence. When it came to artists, this was focused on natural endowments versus trained skill, the relationship between the mind and the hand, and—especially among humanists—whether pictorial art was capable of intelligent authorship as opposed to mere replication of the visible world. Taking Hans Holbein the Younger as a case study, this lecture will explore how the mindful hand of a supremely gifted painter could demonstrate the inherent ingenuity and playful wit of an inventive--rather than merely mimetic--artistic intelligence. 

 

Alexander Marr is University Professor of Renaissance and Early Modern Art. He specializes in European art 1400-1800, especially its intellectual and literary aspects in their social contexts. His most recent publication is Holbein's Wit: Pictorial Ingenuity in Renaissance Art.

 

Before coming to Cambridge, he taught at the University of Southern California and the University of St Andrews. From 2014 to 2019, he was Director of the project Genius before Romanticism: Ingenuity in Early Modern Art & Science, funded by an ERC Consolidator Grant. His awards include a Paul Mellon Centre Senior Fellowship, the Robert H. Smith Residency at the V&A, and a Philip Leverhulme Prize. He was the founding Director of Cambridge Visual Culture (CVC). In 2024, he delivered the Pharos Lectures at the University of Oxford.

 

Through a generous gift to the UNC Arts and Sciences Foundation, William G. Rand established this lecture series in memory of his late wife, Bettie Allison Rand. This funding enables the Department of Art and Art History to invite one or more eminent art historians to UNC-CH every other year for residencies of various lengths. While they are in Chapel Hill, these scholars present a series of lectures and interact with undergraduate and graduate art history and studio art students.

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: *IN-PERSON* SF/F Group
description:
Durham Writers Group
We will be at the People's Solidarity Hub at 1809 Chapel Hill Rd, Durham. This venue does not serve food or drink, but feel free to bring your own. There is a kitchenette for our use, but be sure to clean up afterwards. The space might be a little cozy; please consider masking or staying home if you have a respiratory ailment.

This sub-group focuses on Speculative Fiction, including Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror. If you have anything that falls under that category — be it short story, poem, novel-in-progress or screenplay — then come! We'd love to hear from you.

Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. To ensure fairness, each attendee is limited to 1 minute of Initial Feedback time. During that period, the author remains silent. Next, we have a 5 minute Free-For-All discussion about the work -- then the author may speak. (We usually get through three readers.)

Though not required, in order to receive more in-depth feed-back, readers may post their work in advance on our Google Group:
https://groups.google.com/d/forum/durham-sff-writers-group

We ask that participants keep their comments constructive and respectful, focusing on what works or doesn't work in the piece.

We also ask that readers provide a warning, both on the Google Group and during the meeting, if their story features content that some readers might find upsetting. This includes descriptions of violence or sexual content.

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: Managing Worry and Anxiety
description:
Worries are thoughts we have about the future that generate fear. They arrive in the form of a “what if?” and generate dire warnings about terrible consequences that await us. Unfortunately, these warnings we give ourselves are generally overblown and focused on hypothetical problems that probably won’t happen. Chronic worry that begins to impact the quality of life becomes “anxiety,” and well-intended suggestions to “stop worrying” or applying common stress management techniques are mostly ineffective.

title: Context Over Compute: The Overlooked Lever for AI ROI
description:
Data Science Raleigh
Most enterprises chasing AI ROI look first at bigger models and more compute—but the biggest gains often come from a more economical, less glamorous lever: better context. Pilots stall and production systems underperform not because the models aren't capable, but because they aren't given the right information at the right time, forcing costly rework, manual review, and lost trust.

This webinar reframes context engineering as a business decision rather than a purely technical one. We'll unpack where context investment delivers outsized returns compared to model upgrades, how to identify where context gaps are silently draining value from existing AI initiatives, and how leading teams are prioritizing context work to accelerate time-to-value.

**Key Takeaways:**

1️⃣ **The Real ROI Driver:** Why context—not raw model power—is often the fastest path to measurable AI returns.

2️⃣ **Diagnosing Hidden Costs:** How to spot context gaps that quietly inflate rework, review, and support costs.

3️⃣ **Prioritization Frameworks:** How to decide where to invest in context versus other AI improvements.

4️⃣ **Scaling Value:** Strategies for sustaining ROI gains as AI initiatives expand across the business.

**[Register here](https://datasciconnect.com/events/webinars/context-over-compute/)**

title: Coping During Uncertain Times
description:
People have a powerful need to understand and predict their environments in order to feel in control. When we are exposed to potential threats to our well-being, we naturally respond to this uncertainty with anxiety and fear. This training will address ways of effectively coping with uncertainty in today’s media-saturated world. The course will examine how to remain positive and functional despite the risks of living in a changing world. Included will be practical tips for coping with uncertainty, re-establishing control and how to speak to children about fear.

Please join our virtual welcome session with this link

Are you a young person between 13 and 25 years old who is interested in taking action around preventing gun violence? Join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session to learn more about the different ways you can engage. 

Team ENOUGH is a youth-led program whose mission is to educate young voices about gun violence and mobilize them to take meaningful action against it. Supported by Brady United, we harness the expertise and experience of today’s youth to advance our intersectional work across the country. 

Led by an Executive Council, comprised of students just like us, we believe that diversity is a strength, and that only when everyone has a seat at the table can we build an effective movement to prevent all gun violence in all communities.

For us, preventing gun violence not only requires regulating access to firearms but also addressing how systemic racism and environmental factors cause this form of bloodshed to run especially rampant in communities of color. You cannot talk about gun violence without talking about police brutality, white supremacy, the broken criminal justice system, poverty, homophobia, access to affordable housing, or the often barriers separating disadvantaged populations from physical and mental healthcare. 

So if you share this belief, join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session and become part of the movement to end gun violence in our lifetime.

title: Nov 5 - Visual AI Agriculture Meetup
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics at the intersection of agriculture and AI.

**Date, Time and Location**

Nov 05, 2026
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/visual-ai-agriculture-meetup-november-5-2026)**

Talks will include:

**U-Net Framework for Micro-Scale Surface Damage Segmentation in High-Resolution Soybean Seed Imagery**

Accurate detection of surface-level seed damage is critical for soybean seed quality assurance, yet automated micro-scale damage detection in high-resolution imagery remains an open challenge due to extreme spatial variability in damage scale, severe class imbalance across damage types, and the computational demands of processing ultra-high resolution agricultural imagery at scale. This research addresses the semantic segmentation of fine-grained soybean seed surface defects, such as wrinkles, dark spots, and general surface damage, in 6048 × 4024 pixel images where target damages can be as small as 18 × 18 pixels, using an augmented dataset of 77,000 individual seed images.

To overcome the difficulties of micro-scale detection, spatial sparsity, and class confusion, we propose a two-stage training and dual model inference framework built on an optimized U-Net architecture with a ResNet34 encoder. In the first stage, a damage specialist model is trained using weighted loss functions and a class-balanced approach that prioritizes damage classes.

In the second stage, transfer learning is applied to initialize a healthy seed specialist model from Stage 1 weights, with rebalanced class weights and tile probabilities that identify healthy seeds. During inference, a confidence-gated damage filter suppresses low-confidence predictions, and healthy seed labels are assigned only when the specialist model's confidence exceeds that of the damage model.

The two specialist models achieve validation accuracies of 94% and 98.53%, respectively, and the combined inference system successfully detects and localizes all three damage categories across unseen test images under conditions of extreme spatial variability and class imbalance. Qualitative evaluation confirms close alignment of predicted boundaries with ground truth annotations across all damage types, including dark spots.

These results demonstrate that confidence-gated dual model inference can reduce class confusion in imbalanced micro-scale segmentation, advancing the feasibility of fine-grained automated seed quality inspection at the scale.

*About the Speaker*

[Saurav Upadhyaya](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sauravupadhyaya/) is an AI/ML researcher with a Master's degree in Computer Science, whose work spans agricultural AI, conversational systems, and public health, consistently translating advanced technology into tangible real-world impact.

**From camera to drone: wildfire detection and integration at the edge**

Wildfires are getting larger and more expensive every year. But caught early, a fire is a small job for a small team; caught late, nothing stops it. The cameras to catch them are already installed, so the work is not necessary more sensors but making the ones we have act.

This talk walks the whole chain: a small vision model running on the camera that flags smoke, an integration layer that scores the alert against terrain, weather and history to decide whether it matters, and a drone dispatched to confirm before anyone commits a crew. We will cover what has to run at the edge and why, how small the model can get before it stops seeing smoke, and what it takes to trust a detection nobody has looked at yet.

*About the Speaker*

[Maxime Carriere](https://voxel51.com/events/www.linkedin.com/in/maxime-carriere-871756161) is co-founder of Kernwerk in Berlin, where he works on compressing AI models to run on cheap embedded hardware.

**5,000 Flights to Answer One Question: Can a Drone Sample as Well as a Human?**

Environmental testing still begins with a person walking onto a site with a shovel. We built a system that turns a plain-language brief into a sampling campaign, flies it, and returns soil, water and vegetation samples with GPS, timestamps and chain of custody intact: 5,000 flights, roughly 9,000 miles and 570 flight hours over a 185-acre site in Roatan, much of it under canopy where GPS degrades and clearances are tight.

I will walk through the vision and planning stack, including multispectral and thermal canopy sensing, terrain and land-cover mapping, and the constraint solver that clears a route against airspace and battery budget before anything leaves the ground. Then the harder problem: evidentiary comparability.

A drone-collected result means nothing to a regulator unless it agrees with a hand-collected split under the same method, so I will show the dual-collection protocol we designed to test exactly that. I will close on why calibrated uncertainty and knowing when a model should refuse to answer matter more than raw accuracy once the output lands in a regulatory filing.

*About the Speaker*

[Rohan Talwadia](https://www.linkedin.com/in/rohantalwadia/) is co-founder and CTO of LabGPT, which automates environmental field sampling using drones and edge analysis, with results returned through ISO/IEC 17025-accredited partner laboratories.

title: Hanes Visiting Artist Lecture Series: Sheida Soleimani
location: Hamilton Hall, 100
description:
Department of Art and Art History

 

Sheida Soleimani is an Iranian-American artist who lives in Providence. The daughter of political refugees who were persecuted by the Iranian government in the early 1980s, Soleimani makes work that melds sculpture, collage and photography and highlights her own critical perspective on historical and contemporary socio-political occurrences in Iran. She focuses on media trends and the dissemination of societal occurrences in the news, adapting images from popular press and social media leaks to exist within alternate scenarios. Her work has been recognized internationally in both exhibitions and publications such as Artforum, The New York Times, The Huffington Post, Interview, and VICE Magazine.

 

Soleimani is an Associate Professor of Fine Arts at Brandeis University and a 2026 Guggenheim Fellow.

 

An endowment established in 1983 through the generosity of Nancy and Robin Hanes supports the Art Department's Visiting Artist Series. This important program brings both established and emerging artists to campus to discuss their work in public lectures and to offer individual critiques to our M.F.A. students.  The Hanes Visiting Artist series greatly enriches both our academic programs and our outreach to the wider community.  All lectures are free and open to the public.
