title: The Ritual of Belonging: 35 Years of the Friday Center
location: William and Ida Friday Center
description:
Come. Connect. Celebrate.

 

In 1991, UNC President William C. Friday opened the doors to what he called "the citizens' classroom," a place built to make learning and connection open to everyone, with or without a UNC degree. Named for Bill and Ida Friday, two North Carolinians defined by their service to education and public life, the Friday Center was founded on a simple belief: learning never stops.

For 35 years, the Friday Center has carried that belief forward by opening doors, bringing people together, and extending Carolina's knowledge beyond the traditional classroom. It is a place where the University and the community meet, where ideas are shared, relationships are built, and learning becomes part of a larger public life.

This November, we're celebrating 35 years with an evening centered on something that has always been essential to the Friday Center: the power of gathering, and the belonging it creates.

Joining us is Casper ter Kuile, author of The Power of Ritual and co-founder of Sacred Design Lab.

 

THE POWER OF RITUAL

Amidst rising rates of disconnection, what are the rituals that gather us together? How can we deepen our relationships, make meaningful connections, and experience joyful belonging? Join author and co-founder of Sacred Design Lab Casper ter Kuile for an evening's conversation on the power of ritual. You'll explore how to cultivate the containers of connection at home, on campus, and in the wider community. Learn how ritual can weave us back into a fabric of common life.

 

The Evening

6:30pm | Director's reception, join us for refreshments and conversation
7:15pm | Casper's talk, followed by a live Q&A

 

This is a free event, but space is limited, and registration is required to attend.

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

title: Getting Proper about Prompting:  An Introduction to Prompt Engineering for Social Science and Survey Research
description:
Take a glance through recent news or social media and you would be hard-pressed not to see mentions of chatbots and artificial intelligence (AI) methods aimed at generating text, images and other content.  Recent work by Eloundou and colleagues (2023) explored the potential impact of these types of generative AI on labor markets, and survey research, specifically was among the top two most impacted industries.  Professor Andrew Ng has been cited as saying “AI won’t replace human workers, but ‘people that use it will replace people that don’t.’”  Much of the way researchers in the social sciences and survey research are incorporating AI into their workflow involves some type of prompting.  Prompt Engineering approaches along with more nuanced fine tuning approaches are being used and refined to better incorporate more robust approaches for AI incorporation into the research process.  In this short course we will provide an overview of the emerging field of prompt engineering and illustrate how a prompt engineering approach and problem specification mindset can be useful for maximizing the utility of large language models, specifically, within social science.  Concepts and experimental approaches will be illustrated using several real-world, grounded and published work.  The shortcourse also incorporates an experiential component that encourages participants to apply basic concepts that we cover in the course in real-time as we work on exercises together in the later part of the course.

Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students) are required for Zoom link access.

title: “To BEethoven Rather Than To Seem”: Part II | Gut Instinct Chamber Music Project
location: Person Hall
description:
FEATURING

Nicholas DiEguenio, violin
Mimi Solomon, piano

 

PROGRAM

Featuring Allen Anderson’s “Linen,” plus Beethoven Violin Sonatas Nos. 6 and 7

This season, Gut Instinct takes on the large-scale project “To Beethoven Rather Than To Seem,” marking 200 years since Beethoven’s death and 250 since the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Over the course of five concerts, Nicholas DiEugenio and pianist Mimi Solomon will present all ten Beethoven Sonatas on period instruments along with five commissioned works written expressly for them.

 

PARKING

Please plan to arrive early as parking on campus can be tricky. Learn more about parking and directions to UNC-Chapel Hill’s campus.

 

The Gut Instinct Chamber Music Project, now in its third season, is a concert series in the Triangle area which brings UNC-Chapel Hill and Duke University’s historical instrument collections together with artists committed to presenting inspired, visceral, historically informed performances of the 19th-century chamber music repertoire. The series features music of female composers and their artistic circles. The name “Gut Instinct” is a play on words. In 19th-century Europe, the violin, viola, and cello were strung with (sheep) gut.

 

All of the artists collaborating with the Pleyel and Graf pianos at UNC-Chapel Hill (built in 19th-century Paris and Vienna, respectively), as well as the Clementi piano at Duke (early 19th-century England) use these gut string materials. The turn of phrase “gut instinct” also refers to the visceral, accessible nature of the musical performances that this series presents. Our mission is to make “Historically Informed Performance” accessible, relatable, and culturally relevant! We also want to feature these special pianos that are rarely heard by the public, along with great music by female composers which has remained lesser known to the greater public for far too long, and living composers who are keeping our art form alive!

title: Opening Celebration of Grounded by Maya Freelon
location: Gregg Museum of Art & Design
description:
Join us for a fun-filled afternoon at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design to celebrate the opening of Grounded by acclaimed artist Maya Freelon. 

Drawing on her signature use of delicate tissue paper, Freelon transforms the galleries into an immersive environment that honors both fragility and resilience. In Grounded, the red clay and soil of North Carolina become central materials and metaphors, asking us to consider what it means to create sanctuary in uncertain times and how the land itself holds memory, pain, and possibility.

The community celebration will include local organizations highlighting African American heritage and wellness, along with special performances by Tre. Charles, Johnny Lee Chapman III, and NC State’s Panoramic Dance Project. 

You are invited to Connect. Celebrate. Get Grounded. Please read more about the timed activities below.

Celebration Program Schedule

1 p.m. | Celebration Begins

Enjoy ongoing activities throughout the museum and grounds from 1-5 p.m., including a collaborative Tissue Paper Quilting activity inside the Grounded exhibition, community organization tables, a food truck and more. Complimentary non-alcoholic beverages and light treats will be provided. 

1:15–1:45 p.m. | Panoramic Dance
Experience a special performance choreographed by Christa Oliver and featuring NC State students. The performance begins outside the museum’s main entrance, inviting visitors to follow the dancers into the galleries for a brief performance before moving together outdoors. Accessible seating will be available for visitors who need accommodations. The program is primarily designed for standing-room viewing. 

1:45–2:10 p.m. | Welcome and Opening Remarks with artist Maya Freelon
Opening remarks with artist Maya Freelon, Gregg Museum Director Sara Segerlin, and special guests, at the concert stage by the front lawn.

2:15–3:45 p.m. | Tre. Charles concert at the Museum Lawn
Enjoy an outdoor concert on the lawn featuring Tre. Charles and band.  Please feel free to bring a lawn chair or blanket.

2:45–3 p.m. and 3:30–3:45 p.m. | Spoken Word with Johnny Lee Chapman
Raleigh Poet Laureate Johnny Lee Chapman presents two intimate spoken word performances in Crafting Sanctuaries.

3:45–4:15 p.m. | Panoramic Dance
A second opportunity to experience Panoramic Dance with Christa Oliver and NC State students, beginning outside the museum entrance and moving through the galleries and outdoors. Accessible seating will be available for visitors who need accommodations. The program is primarily designed for standing-room viewing. 

5 p.m. | Celebration Concludes 

Parking: The Gregg Museum parking lot will be closed for the celebration. Visitors may park in the Ferndell public parking lot or at Pullen Arts Center, where parking is free on Saturdays. These alternate parking locations are approximately 2–4 blocks from the museum. Please visit the Gregg Museum website for additional parking information: https://gregg.arts.ncsu.edu/about/visit/alternate-parking-locations-for-the-gregg-museum/

Free and open to the public. Please register for the general event, and feel free to drop in anytime between 1 and 5 p.m.
source: NC State Gregg Museum of Art & Design

title: Toshi Reagon EcoTones
location: Memorial Hall
description:
Some performances entertain. Others leave audiences seeing the world differently. In EcoTones, music, storytelling, research, personal history, and lived experience come together in an experience that feels less like a performance and more like a gathering. Warm, joyful, and challenging, the work invites audiences to consider what happens when different worlds meet and what becomes possible in the spaces between them.

 

Inspired by the ecological concept of an ecotone—the place where distinct ecosystems overlap and create the conditions for new life—EcoTones explores the intersections that shape our lives, communities, and futures. The result is a shared act of discovery that reveals unexpected connections and invites audiences to see familiar questions from new perspectives.

 

Created by Toshi Reagon in collaboration with UNC-Chapel Hill scholars Danielle Spurlock and Danielle Purifoy and Durham-based writer, scholar, and activist Alexis Pauline Gumbs, the performance places artists and researchers side by side on stage. Their stories, questions, ideas, and experiences become part of the work itself, reflecting Toshi’s belief that important voices and perspectives in our communities belong in shared public conversation.

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/toshireagon-ecotones/

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: Digital Accessibility Pop-Up Labs
location: Carolina Union, 2502
description:
The POP Lab is a drop-in workspace where UNC faculty and staff can make progress with support from digital accessibility consultants. Bring your documents, course materials, websites, reports, or questions, and work at your own pace. Come by for a few minutes or stay for the full session to ask questions, explore tools, solve problems and make meaningful progress toward expanding access.

 

Progress Over Perfection

Progress means recognizing common barriers in the platforms you use and taking small steps to reduce them. It’s choosing web formats over PDFs, applying table headers, checking color contrast and collaborating on accessible templates so everyone can start from a strong foundation. Digital accessibility depends on steady, intentional progress, not perfection, to expand access for all.

title: GenAI Tools and Resources in the Clinical Setting
description:
Curious about how to use generative AI (genAI) to inform your clinical research and practice?

 

This session will cover the basics of using genAI chatbots and AI-assisted tools for clinical information retrieval and literature reviews. We’ll discuss the pros and cons of using AI tools for different steps of the research process, prompting strategies, and using GenAI for evidence reviews. A review of clinical genAI tools will be included.

 

This workshop is offered by the UNC Health Sciences Library and is led by Luke Barron, Joel Collier, and Beth Moreton. It is part of the For Clinicians: Enhancing Practice Through Knowledge and Advancing Clinical Research Skills workshop tracks.

title: Ackland Film Forum: "Nightcrawler" (Dan Gilroy, 2014)
location: The Lumina Theater, 620 Market Street, Chapel Hill, 27516, United States
description:
Jake Gyllenhaal delivers a career-defining performance as an ambitious freelancer who prowls Los Angeles after dark in search of footage for local television news. The city’s nocturnal landscape of police sirens, flashing lights, and breaking stories becomes the backdrop for a mordant examination of ambition, competition, and media culture in the twenty-first century. 
This film will be introduced by Kino Korner, graduate student association. 
It will be screened at 7:30 p.m. at The Lumina Theater (620 Market St, Chapel Hill, NC 27516). Tickets are free for all audience members, and registration is required via The Lumina’s webpage. When this link is live, click to reserve your free ticket. 
UNC-Chapel Hill students can receive CLE credit for attending by scanning the QR code at the event. 
  
About the Series: 
Join the Ackland Film Forum this fall for Socially Charged Crime Thrillers: Snapshots of Social Anxiety, a series that accompanies the Ackland exhibition Care and Concern: Recent Acquisitions of Modern and Contemporary Art. 
As vehicles of social commentary and stylistic bravura, crime thrillers often register the pressures and contradictions of their historical moment. Across nearly half a century, the films in this series stage encounters with political power, public trust, inequality, and ambition through assassination plots, botched robberies, and media-driven spectacle. 
From the crises of the late 1960s to the intensified media environments of the twenty-first century, these works show how genre cinema can capture social anxiety in real time. Each film stands both as a gripping narrative and as a record of a world under strain, where institutions falter and everyday life becomes fraught with conflict. 
The Ackland Film Forum is co-organized by the Ackland Art Museum and UNC Film Studies, housed in the UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature.

title: Rethinking Seasonal Cleanup: Why Less Can Be More for Wildlife (in person)
location: Duke Gardens–Pelham-Cullen Classroom in the Barnes Welcome Center, 420 Anderson Street, Durham, NC, 27705, United States
description:
Are you unsure about when to cut back dormant plants or how many leaves to leave behind? Perhaps you’ve heard about stem-nesting bees or insects that overwinter in fallen foliage and want to support them. Traditional garden practice dictated raking leaves and cutting everything back to “tidy up” before winter. Today, delaying cutbacks and leaving fallen leaves has become more common as gardeners appreciate plants’ unique winter beauty and prioritize wildlife. The best approach depends on your landscape goals and priorities, and this session will help you navigate seasonal cutbacks and leaf management. Join Shannon Currey, education and outreach at Izel Native Plants, to learn strategies that support local wildlife while maintaining a landscape that looks cared for and intentional. This description is for the in-person attendance option—register separately to attend virtually.

title: Durham Social Hack Night
description:
Triangle Developers
Hey tech folks, come out and hang at Hi-Wire starting at 6pm! Hack Night is meant to be a social evening for folks in tech. It's less about networking and more about community.

**Look for the Hack Night tabletop sign** and nerds wearing name tags to find us. If the weather is nice, we'll probably be outside.

Help folks feel welcome by using the **"Pac Man Rule"** \- when standing with a group of people \(usually in a circle\)\, leave some space open so that another person can easily join\.

See our [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/TriangleDevsSlack/policies/blob/master/code-of-conduct.md). To summarize: be nice or leave. No tolerance for harassment or oppression. In addition, since alcohol is present at these events, please be mindful of your consumption and respect other people's choices on whether or not to consume.

**FAQs**
*Do folks hack at Hack Night? Should I bring my computer?*
This is more of a night for hackers than an actual hack night. You're welcome to bring a laptop, but most people will only be socializing.

*What are the beverage options? Are there any non-alcoholic drinks?*
Hi-Wire Brewing offers many types of beers including a few non-alcoholic options plus wine and some liquor. They usually have a happy hour special on the first few beers on the menu. In the same complex are Cugino Forno which has additional drink options, and Two Roosters which has excellent ice cream.

*Are there any drink specials?*
If Hack Night is on a Tuesday, Hi-Wire usually has $5 pints for their flagship beers. Look for the list at the counter.

*Do people eat snacks/dinner during the meetup?*
Sometimes folks will order a pizza or salad from Cugino Forno. I sometimes grab an ice cream from Two Roosters across the way. Most people eat before or after but it's no big deal - whatever you prefer and are most comfortable with.

*How can I connect with the developer community?*
Go to [triangledevelopers.com](https://triangledevelopers.com/) to find the Discord and Slack info.

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Methods for Conducting Qualitative Coding and Data Analysis
description:
Knowing how to analyze data from qualitative research studies to respond to complex health and social priorities is rewarding, but it can also be daunting. This short course provides students practical skills for coding and analyzing qualitative data for research studies in U.S. and international settings. The short course uses a lab- and discussion-based approach. There will be four modules. In the 1st module, students will learn about the practical steps for qualitative coding and data analysis, including learning about concepts and techniques relating to how to iteratively read narrative data, how to develop codes, how to create a codebook, how to consider hierarchal coding structures, and how to formulate themes from codes. As part of this module, students will also learn about three types of analytical approaches: content analysis, thematic analysis, and discourse analysis. In the 2nd module, students will learn about how to use an online qualitative analysis software tool, including how to import a qualitative dataset and codebook and how to assign codes to text. We will review a real-world example of a coded qualitative dataset to discuss techniques for obtaining code extracts, memos, matrices, and other analytical tools. In the 3rd module, students will read three qualitative transcripts from a topic selected by the instructor and work in small groups to develop an abbreviated codebook and assign codes to the test transcripts. Students will work in real-time using an online qualitative analysis software. In the final module, students will learn about various ways to present findings from qualitative data analyses. We will critique and discuss various styles for presenting qualitative research, such as using illustrative quotations, visual displays, or quantified qualitative results. Students will learn about the inherent advantages and disadvantages of these styles when presenting their own qualitative findings. This course is designed to provide new knowledge for both introductory and intermediate students.

Registration and fee are required for Zoom link access.

title: Nov 11 - AI, ML and Computer Vision Meetup
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics across AI, ML, and computer vision.

**Time, Date and Location**

Nov 11, 2026
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/ai-ml-and-computer-vision-meetup-november-11-2026)**

**Agentic RAG: Beyond Retrieve-and-Generate**

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the default pattern for grounding large language models in external knowledge, but most implementations still follow a rigid retrieve-once, generate-once pipeline — one that struggles with multi-hop questions, ambiguous queries, and knowing when its own retrieved context is insufficient. This talk introduces Agentic RAG, where retrieval is treated as an action within an agent's reasoning loop rather than a fixed upstream step.

We'll examine query decomposition and routing for breaking complex questions into targeted sub-queries, self-reflective and corrective retrieval loops that let an agent judge and re-query its own results, and tool-orchestration patterns (via MCP) that let retrieval sit alongside other agent actions like database lookups and API calls. Using a live architecture — evolving a standard RAG chatbot into an agentic, MCP-connected system — we'll walk through what changes in design, and where these systems introduce new failure modes: grounding drift, latency and cost from repeated retrieval loops, and cases where a simpler RAG pipeline still wins.

Attendees will leave with a practical framework for deciding when the added complexity of agentic RAG is worth it, and a set of design patterns for building it correctly.

*About the Speaker*

[Balaji Venkatasubramaniyar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/balaji-venkatasubramaniyar/) is a Technical Lead at Wisdom Infotech, leading a 15+ person engineering team delivering enterprise solutions. With 13+ years of experience in enterprise software and insurance technology, he specializes in agentic AI systems, RAG architectures, and vector databases.

**GeoAI for the Physical World: Earth Observation, Foundation Models, and Urban Digital Twins**

Earth observation provides a unique form of computer vision for understanding the physical world at city to continental scales. In this talk, I will show how satellite imagery, geospatial data, machine learning, and foundation-model representations can be combined to characterize urban environments and environmental conditions.

I will present UrbanScope Open, an open GeoAI digital-twin prototype integrating Earth observation with 3D buildings, vegetation, land-surface temperature, air quality, noise, population, and other urban data. I will also share lessons from my research using geospatial foundation-model embeddings for environmental prediction across Europe.

The talk will discuss how these approaches can contribute to increasingly multimodal AI systems capable of reasoning about real-world environments.

*About the Speaker*

[Cesar Alvarez](https://voxel51.com/events/cesar.alvarez@uni-a.de) is a researcher at the University of Augsburg working at the intersection of GeoAI, Earth observation, remote sensing, and environmental intelligence. His research applies machine learning, computer vision, and geospatial foundation models to problems including urban environments, climate risk, air quality, and agriculture.

**Can agents get curious?**

Most AI agents are good at answering a question once we tell them exactly what to look for. The harder problem is building agents that can explore a complex dataset autonomously: generating hypotheses, deciding which analyses are worth running, allocating additional compute when evidence is ambiguous, and knowing when they have enough evidence to stop.

In this talk, I’ll show an architecture for autonomous research agents that combines structured knowledge, iterative tool use, and explicit evidence tracking to turn open-ended questions into a sequence of testable investigations. I’ll discuss practical lessons from building and evaluating these systems, including why more test-time compute does not automatically produce better research and how provenance and evaluation can make long-running agents more reliable.

I’ll close with a live example of an agent exploring a dataset, revising its hypotheses, and choosing what to investigate next.

*About the Speaker*

[Srivatsa P](https://www.linkedin.com/in/srivatsa-p) is a member of technical staff at Sigma Computing, where he works on AI agents that reason over complex enterprise data. Previously, he worked on machine learning at Apple and conducted research at the MIT Media Lab; outside of traditional ML, he has also worked on mapping coral reefs through underwater imaging, which sparked an enduring interest in how intelligent systems make sense of messy real-world data.
source: Meetup: Raleigh AI, ML & Computer Vision

title: Business Context in AI Initiatives: Why It Matters More Than You Think
description:
Data Science Raleigh
AI initiatives depend on data—but data without business context can lead to inconsistent answers, unreliable insights, and decisions that miss the mark.

What does “customer,” “revenue,” or even “active” actually mean across your organization? The answer can vary by team, system, or business function.

While these inconsistencies have long created challenges for data and analytics teams, the rise of AI makes the stakes even higher.

In this expert panel, moderated by Jennifer Jackson, Chief Marketing Officer at Actian, we’ll explore why business context has become a critical foundation for trusted AI. Hear perspectives on how organizations can align definitions, metrics, ownership, and relationships across their data environment—and make that context accessible to the AI experiences employees and leaders increasingly rely on.

The session will also feature a live walkthrough demonstrating how modern data platforms can activate business metrics and context with less manual effort, along with practical questions to consider when evaluating whether your data and AI foundation is ready to scale.

**What You'll Learn:**

1️⃣ Why business context matters beyond traditional data and technical teams

2️⃣ How incomplete, inconsistent, or siloed business definitions can impact AI initiatives

3️⃣ How trusted and up-to-date business context can improve the relevance and reliability of AI-driven insights

4️⃣ What it looks like to operationalize business context without creating additional manual overhead

5️⃣ Key questions to ask when evaluating your organization's data and AI readiness

**Who Should Attend**

Business, data, analytics, and technology leaders responsible for developing, scaling, or operationalizing AI initiatives.

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Introduction to Constructivist Grounded Theory
description:
This course introduces participants to constructivist grounded theory (CGT). Grounded theory (GT) methods consist of flexible guidelines to fit particular research problems, not to apply mechanically. With these guidelines, you expedite and systematize data collection and analysis. GT methods can assist researchers in making their work more analytic, precise, and compelling.

In this course, following an exploration of the history and development of GT, we examine GT basic guidelines and major strategies, including initial line-by-line and focused coding, the use of gerunds, memoing, diagramming, theoretical sampling, and categorizing. Throughout the sessions, there is an emphasis on CGT’s epistemological foundation and resultant adaptations to the research process, including regarding the literature review, researcher positionality/ies and reflexivity, and participant involvement.

The course will include a number of hands-on exercises to exemplify, and give participants an opportunity to practice, the strategies being discussed. For the coding exercise, you may bring and use some of your own qualitative data, or if you do not have data yet, some will be supplied. Clear guidelines and support are provided to course participants with regard to all aspects of CGT.

The sessions will utilize CGT readings and resources from Kathy Charmaz, Robert Thornberg, Adele Clarke, and myself, and will draw on the extensive scholarship of Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss. A pack of materials will be shared with participants in advance of the course. This course will be of interest to those doing full CGT studies but also to those who may be interested in learning about and potentially using some of the powerful GT strategies (such as coding) in studies with a different overall methodological approach.

Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students) are required for Zoom link access.

title: Sankai Juku TOTEM: Void and Height
location: Memorial Hall
description:
Sankai Juku creates work that unfolds slowly and deliberately, into what can feel like a new world, where forces like time and gravity seem to act on us in radically new ways.

 

In TOTEM: Void and Height, dancers move with extraordinary presence and precision. Practicing the Japanese dance tradition of Butoh, the company’s performances exist somehow between stillness and action, between gravity and transcendence—and sometimes feel less like watching dance and more like stepping inside a waking dream. 

 

The final work choreographed by their founder Ushio Amagatsu before his death in 2024, TOTEM: Void and Height reflects a lifelong exploration of the relationship between the human body, the natural world, and the forces that shape them both. Through striking imagery and breathtaking physical control, the performance invites audiences to slow down, pay attention, and experience time differently.

 

This is a rare opportunity to encounter one of the world’s most influential contemporary dance companies and the final artistic vision of the artist who shaped it for more than five decades.

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/totem/

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu 

 

Image credit: Courtesy of the artist

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu 

 

Image credit: Courtesy of the artist

title: Biomimicry: Nature as a Mentor
location: Swift Creek Bluffs Nature Preserve, 7800 Holly Springs Rd, Raleigh, NC, 27606, United States
description:
Learn about biomimicry at Swift Creek Bluffs!
Biomimicry (from the Greek bios, meaning life, and mimesis, meaning to imitate) is the practice of looking at how plants, animals, and ecosystems solve problems and then copying those designs to solve human challenges. It’s not about using nature as a resource (like cutting down trees for wood); it’s about learning from nature as a mentor. 

Join Hike Leader, Leigh Aultman, for a morning of Biological Storytelling. We will walk the short creek loop trail with up to six stops where stories will be shared about local organisms' biological adaptations and how those adaptations and innovations can inform human designs.  This is a free event, but preregistration is required. Due to the size of the parking lot, we will keep the hiking group small and ask that you register by vehicle rather than individual. Feel free to bring guests but please carpool to ensure we have enough space in the parking lot.

location: 114 - living room
description: This event is intended for Queer and/or Trans survivors:Some of the biggest barriers to survivor safety are finance related. title: 2026 Stone Memorial Lecture by Dr. Alexis Pauline Gumbs
location: The Sonja Haynes Stone Center for Research in Black Culture and History, Stone Center Auditorium
description:
Lecture Title: A Homemade Field of Love: Expansive Understandings of Growth in Times of Change


Description: Community cherished Black feminist writer and scholar Alexis Pauline Gumbs will lead an interactive lecture inspired by the “field” as a form of life, from a field of collard greens, to the quantum field. These mediations on “the field” are inspired by her research on June Jordan, Fannie Lou Hamer, George Washington Carver and her most recent book Primary: After and With Alma Thomas. And what fertilizes it all is the legacy of Sonja Haynes Stone whom this lecture celebrates as a founder of the infinitely possible field of Black Studies.

 

Dr. Alexis Pauline Gumbs is a Queer Black Feminist Love Evangelist and an aspirational favorite cousin to all life. Her work in this lifetime is to facilitate infinite, unstoppable ancestral love in practice. Alexis’ books are portable textual ceremonies. Her most recent book Survival is a Promise: The Eternal Life of Audre Lorde revolutionizes the scale of life writing. Her award-winning meditation Undrowned: Black Feminist Lessons from Marine Mammals offers the critical interspecies love song we need at this urgent stage of our collective evolution. Alexis is also currently working her next book in honor of June Jordan and Fannie Lou Hamer, A Homemade Field of Love (forthcoming from Yale University Press). Alexis is currently a Monument Lab Fellow and a Loss and Damage Collaborative Commissioned Author creating ceremony in honor of the wisdom of climate catastrophe survivors in the legacy of Audre Lorde. Alexis received a 2023 Windham Campbell Prize Winner in Poetry, 2022 Whiting Award in Nonfiction and a 2022 National Endowment for the Arts Fellowship in Prose. Alexis was also a 2020-2021 National Humanities Center Fellow. She has transformed the scope of intellectual, creative and oracular writing with her triptych of experimental works published by Duke University Press (Spill: Scenes of Black Feminist Fugitivity in 2016, M Archive: After the End of the World in 2018 and Dub: Finding Ceremony in 2020.) Unlike most academic texts, Alexis’s work has inspired artists across form to create dance works, installation work, paintings, processionals, divination practices, operas, quilts and more.

 

Read more about the speaker: www.alexispauline.com

Register now: https://go.unc.edu/StoneMemorialLecture

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Methods for Navigating the U.S. Health and Social Sciences Job Market
description:
Knowing how to competitively differentiate oneself to obtain a new job in the U.S. health and social sciences field is important, but not always easy to figure out. This short course provides students with practical tips and insights on how to competitively apply for public health professional jobs in the U.S. relating to research, practice, or policy. The course also focuses on U.S. jobs in the social sciences. There will be four modules. In the 1st module, students will learn about best practices for writing cover letters and curriculum vitae (CVs), preparing for interviews, following up on interviews, integrating non-traditional work and volunteer experiences on one’s CV, integrating coursework skills, and negotiating salaries within a human resource lens. As part of this module, students will also learn about how some health and social sciences positions are funded in order to understand how best to respond to active job postings or how best to pursue job opportunities within professional networks. In the 2nd module, students will review strengths and recommendations for improving a selected set of anonymous CVs. As part of this exercise, students will have the option of submitting their CV one week prior to the short course for the instructor to anonymize, including removing identifying information such as name and contact information. With each student’s prior permission, the instructor and class will share during the short course what they understood and did not understand about the anonymized CV, including suggestions for how to enhance the CV. This is a rare opportunity to hear firsthand how other professionals consume your CV and find out what they deemed to be the most and least valuable components. After the discussion, the CV holder will have the option of revealing themself (or not) to query the instructor and course peers regarding any additional insights. In the 3rd module, students will learn about contemporary approaches to marketing oneself when applying for jobs, including the potential advantages of leveraging personal webpages, professional network sites, conference meetings, business cards, referrals, informational interviews, or social media. We will also discuss several do’s and don’ts. In the final module, students will learn about ways to stay organized and motivated during a job search, including developing a plan relating to the number and type of job positions to apply to and how to fill in possible gaps in one’s CV. This course is designed to provide new knowledge for both students and professionals who are recent graduates of Master’s or doctoral degree programs in health and social sciences.

Registration and fee are required for Zoom link access.

Ballet BC transforms a theater full of strangers into a single, collective audience response—a gasp, a silence, a moment of awe.

 

This triple bill explores what it means to be human in relationship to one another, moving from the vulnerable to the virtuosic, exploring deeply personal stories and moments of quiet intimacy to the exhilaration of masses of bodies moving together as one. 

 

The evening opens with Obsidian by choreographic collaborators Bobbi Jene Smith and Or Schraiber, whose work has been described as “wild and rebellious.” Artistic Director Medhi Walerski’s SWAY follows, inspired by Emily Dickinson’s poem “Hope is the thing with feathers” and set to an original score by Adrien Cronet, creating moments as fleeting and precarious as the hope described in the poem. The evening concludes with Shahar Binyamini’s BOLERO X, set to Ravel’s Boléro, that builds with pulsating drive and excitement as the ranks of Ballet BC dancers multiply their forces, turning the stage into a sweeping, euphoric, collective—and culminating in a finale so extraordinary that a room full of strangers can’t help but respond together.

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/balletbc/

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Nov 19 - Visualizing and Debugging Hugging Face's LeRobot Data
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
This workshop is a hands-on tour of what actually breaks when you load real LeRobot datasets, and how Voxel51's native LeRobot support in FiftyOne catches it.

**Date, Time and Location**

Nov 19, 2026
9:00 AM - 10:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/lerobot-workshop-november-19-2026)**

Robot learning data doesn't look like the data that trains most vision-language models. It's temporal, low-dimensional in the parts that matter most, embodiment-specific, and expensive to collect, and increasingly, it's shipped in Hugging Face's LeRobot format. But packaging robot data consistently isn't the same as being able to see it: episodes hide broken metadata, silently dropped sensor modalities, and mismatched schemas between robots that look identical on paper.

Starting from the core differences that make robot data hard (temporal structure, proprioception, action grounding, embodiment heterogeneity, data scarcity), we'll move into live debugging: a metadata bug that broke multiple dataset imports, sensor streams that vanish without an error, and two robots running an identical benchmark whose data is structurally incompatible. By the end, you'll know what to check before you trust a LeRobot dataset, and how to actually look inside one.
source: Meetup: Raleigh AI, ML & Computer Vision

title: Carolina History Tour
description:
Learn more about the history of the nation’s first public university by attending a Carolina History Tour. The Carolina History Tours cover more than 200 years of the history of UNC-Chapel Hill, including the establishment of the university in the 18th century, the history of campus landmarks including the Old Well, Davie Poplar, and Unsung Founders Memorial, the push to open enrollment to all North Carolinians, and the growth of the school in the 20th and 21st centuries. Tours will begin at the Old Well and finish at Wilson Library. Most tours last a little over an hour. 

Led by staff from the Wilson Special Collections Library, these tours are part of the University Library’s commitment to collecting, preserving, and sharing the history of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu 

 

Image credit: Courtesy of the artist

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu 

 

Image credit: Courtesy of the artist

How to join:
Please join our virtual welcome session with this link

Are you a young person between 13 and 25 years old who is interested in taking action around preventing gun violence? Join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session to learn more about the different ways you can engage. 

Team ENOUGH is a youth-led program whose mission is to educate young voices about gun violence and mobilize them to take meaningful action against it. Supported by Brady United, we harness the expertise and experience of today’s youth to advance our intersectional work across the country. 

Led by an Executive Council, comprised of students just like us, we believe that diversity is a strength, and that only when everyone has a seat at the table can we build an effective movement to prevent all gun violence in all communities.

For us, preventing gun violence not only requires regulating access to firearms but also addressing how systemic racism and environmental factors cause this form of bloodshed to run especially rampant in communities of color. You cannot talk about gun violence without talking about police brutality, white supremacy, the broken criminal justice system, poverty, homophobia, access to affordable housing, or the often barriers separating disadvantaged populations from physical and mental healthcare. 

So if you share this belief, join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session and become part of the movement to end gun violence in our lifetime.

We are excited to see you soon!

* A step-by-step walkthrough of our Phone Dialer tools.

* Opportunities to ask questions and connect with other like-minded volunteers.

title: Hip Hop Nutcracker
location: Durham Performing Arts Center (DPAC), 123 Vivian Street / William V. 'Bill' Bell Way, Durham, NC, 27701, United States
description:
A holiday mash-up for the whole family, The Hip Hop Nutcracker returns for another spectacular tour. Directed and choreographed by Tony and Olivier Award-nominated Jennifer Weber, this contemporary dance spectacle is a re-mixed and re-imagined version of the classic, smashing hip hop dance and Tchaikovsky’s timeless music together into a heart-stirring and inspirational holiday event. The Hip Hop Nutcracker is brought to life by a powerhouse cast of a dozen all-star dancers, a DJ, a violinist, and MC Kurtis Blow, one of hip hop’s founding fathers, who opens the show with a short set.

Just like the original, in The Hip Hop Nutcracker, Maria-Clara and the Nutcracker Prince go on a dream adventure battling a gang of mice, visiting the land of sweets and learning the lessons of the holiday season. Innovative digital graffiti and visuals transform the landscape of E.T.A. Hoffmann’s beloved story from traditional 19th Century Germany to the vibrant, diverse sights and sounds of contemporary New York City.

Grab your family and friends and let the dynamic performers of The Hip Hop Nutcracker take you on a journey that celebrates love, community and the magic of the holiday season. Get your tickets here!

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu 

 

Image credit: Courtesy of the artist

title: “Learning from Electric Lady,” presented by John Storyk, Award Winning Studio Designer
location: Hill Hall, Moeser Auditorium
description:
“Learning from Electric Lady”
Noted architect and acoustician John Storyk will be on campus for a presentation on his lifetime career for the professional audio and video recording community, highlighting his work in studio design, including new projects and ideas about where the studio design world is headed.

 

A registered architect and acoustician, John Storyk and wife Beth Walters are the founding partners of WSDG. The firm has provided acoustic and AV technology consulting and design services since the groundbreaking 1969 design of Jimi Hendrix’s Electric Lady Studios in New York City.

 

John received his architectural studies from Princeton and Columbia Universities. As an designer, engineer and principal of WSDG he has been responsible for over 3000 world-class audio/video production facilities, including studios, radio stations, video suites, entertainment clubs and theaters. His work includes private studios for Whitney Houston, Bob Marley, Ace Frehley, Stevie Wonder, Paul Epworth, Jack Antonoff, Bruce Springsteen, Alicia Keys, J. Cole, Greenday, Harry Connick, JR, JZ and others. Professional audio video installations include Soundshop (Nashville); Crawford Post (Atlanta); Talking House (San Francisco); Rue Boyer (Paris), Sony (LA), Spotify (LA); Jungle Studios (NYC); KEXP Radio (Seatle); Jazz at Lincoln Center (NYC); UCLA – Lani Hall (Los Angeles); and Berklee College of Music (Boston).

 

John is a member of the American Institute of Architects (AIA), Acoustical Society of America, Audio Engineering Society (AES) and a frequent contributor to AES convention papers and professional industry periodicals. He is a frequent lecturer at schools throughout the nation and has established courses in acoustics at several universities, including Berklee College of Music, where he is a long time adjunct professor of acoustics and studio design.

 

He and the 60 person global WSDG team are a 13-time winner of the NAMM TEC award for studio design.

 

This event is free and open to the public. Students can earn CLE credit for attending.

We will focus on the most urgent campaigns that need our help. Some of these campaigns may include stopping bills that will make it harder for millions of Americans—especially students, seniors, and veterans—to cast their ballots. We need your help to ensure voters across the country call their state representatives and demand they protect the freedom to vote.

No prior experience is necessary—our team will provide full training at the start of each shift!

* A step-by-step walkthrough of our Phone Dialer tools.
* Expert tips on effective communication with voters.
* Opportunities to ask questions and connect with other like-minded volunteers.


Sign up today and take the first step toward empowering voters and protecting democracy in 2025!

description:
Durham Writers Group
We will be at the Moon House at 3039 University Dr. in Durham. This venue does not serve food or drink, but feel free to bring your own. There is a kitchenette for our use, but be sure to clean up afterwards. The space might be a little cozy; please consider masking or staying home if you have a respiratory ailment.

This sub-group focuses on Speculative Fiction, including Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror. If you have anything that falls under that category — be it short story, poem, novel-in-progress or screenplay — then come! We'd love to hear from you.

Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. To ensure fairness, each attendee is limited to 1 minute of Initial Feedback time. During that period, the author remains silent. Next, we have a 5 minute Free-For-All discussion about the work -- then the author may speak. (We usually get through three readers.)

Though not required, in order to receive more in-depth feed-back, readers may post their work in advance on our Google Group:

We ask that participants keep their comments constructive and respectful, focusing on what works or doesn't work in the piece.

We also ask that readers provide a warning, both on the Google Group and during the meeting, if their story features content that some readers might find upsetting. This includes descriptions of violence or sexual content.

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and gallery talk: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light explores how powerful emotions can be expressed through simplicity. Using bold contrasts between light and dark, the artist creates striking images that convey feeling through form, space, and gesture rather than detailed storytelling. The exhibition invites viewers to slow down and experience mood, tension, and vulnerability in a direct and deeply human way.

 

Weight of Light brings together seven works created by artist taylor barnes during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. The work marks a period of experimentation and personal reflection. Drawing from her background in fibers and ceramics, barnes approaches the canvas as a site of material exploration. Through processes of staining, layering, and transforming solids into liquids and back again, she creates environments that make space for chance, absence, and emergence. The seven works resist Western linear narratives, instead functioning as maps of origin within an ongoing movement from uncertainty towards revelation. Moving between darkness and light, the works consider perception, ambiguity, and the experience of reclaiming. Existing somewhere between painting and object, these works function as thresholds. As open-ended structures, Weight of Light positions ascension as a practice of self-possession and power.

 

taylor barnes is a ceramicist and fiber artist exploring spirituality, oral history, and power through material and form. Heavily influenced by bell hooks' object/subject theories, she works with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal to translate emotion and experience into tangible presence. Black being her only color choice and philosophy, she creates work that appears restrained yet carries deep labor, lineage, ritual, and quiet intensity. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/

Please join our virtual welcome session with this link

Are you a young person between 13 and 25 years old who is interested in taking action around preventing gun violence? Join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session to learn more about the different ways you can engage. 

Team ENOUGH is a youth-led program whose mission is to educate young voices about gun violence and mobilize them to take meaningful action against it. Supported by Brady United, we harness the expertise and experience of today’s youth to advance our intersectional work across the country. 

Led by an Executive Council, comprised of students just like us, we believe that diversity is a strength, and that only when everyone has a seat at the table can we build an effective movement to prevent all gun violence in all communities.

For us, preventing gun violence not only requires regulating access to firearms but also addressing how systemic racism and environmental factors cause this form of bloodshed to run especially rampant in communities of color. You cannot talk about gun violence without talking about police brutality, white supremacy, the broken criminal justice system, poverty, homophobia, access to affordable housing, or the often barriers separating disadvantaged populations from physical and mental healthcare. 

So if you share this belief, join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session and become part of the movement to end gun violence in our lifetime.
